Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 506 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit 506 (WMU) covers an 
area of 2,189 km² and is located in north-central 
Alberta, in the Boreal Dry Mixedwood natural 
subregion. 
Agriculture is the predominant land use (50%) in WMU 
506, with broadleaf forests interspersed amongst 
coniferous forests, shrubland, and grasslands. 
Approximately 450 km² of land in the Tawatinaw River 
valley has a provincial land use designation as ‘Key 
Wildlife Biodiversity Zone’. Given their localized size 
and distribution, Key Wildlife Biodiversity Zones play a 
disproportionately large role in maintaining overall 
productivity of regional ungulate populations and are a 
source of biodiversity. These zones ensure that 
significant proportions of the breeding population 
survive to the next year (Environment and Sustainable 
Resource Development 2015). 
The objective of the 2025 aerial ungulate survey was 
to assess the status of ungulate populations (moose, 
white-tailed deer, and mule deer if adequate 
observations were obtained) in WMU 506 by estimating 
abundance, density, and the age-sex composition. 
Survey Method 
An aerial survey for ungulates was conducted 
February 6–7, 2025 using distance sampling 
techniques (Alberta Environment and Parks 2016, 
Buckland et al. 2001, Thomas et al. 2010). A total of 42 
north-south transect lines spaced 1.2 km apart were flown 
with one Astar helicopter (Airbus AS350 SD2) for a total 
survey effort of 406 km. Ungulates were classified as 
male or female and by age class (adult or juvenile) 
when possible. Female moose were identified 
primarily by the presence of a vulva patch. White-tailed 
deer were classified as male if antlers were present, 
and female if antlers were absent and accompanied by 
a juvenile. It is assumed that most males have cast 
antlers when late winter aerial surveys occur (Alberta 
Sustainable Resource Development 2010). The 
categories of ungulate activity (bedded, standing, 
moving), and canopy cover (0–33%, 34–66%, and 
>66%) within 10 m of the ungulate, were included as
covariates to improve estimates associated with the
survey. Other wildlife sightings were recorded,
including 23 mule deer and 21 elk.
Results 
Moo
se 
A total of 105 moose were observed in 59 groups and 
classified as 27 bulls, 57 cows, and 21 calves. The 
estimated bull:cow:calf ratio was 48:100:37. The 
estimated density was 0.341 moose/km² (90% 
Confidence Interval (CI) 0.258–0.450; Coefficient of 
Variation (CV) = 17.0%) and the estimated abundance 
was 745 moose (90% CI 564–986; CV = 17.0%). 
Results are summarized in Table 1. 
Wh
ite-tailed deer 
A total of 203 white-tailed deer were observed in 51 
groups and classified as 10 bucks (all with antlers), 8 
does, 15 fawns, and 170 unclassified. The estimated 
buck:doe:fawn ratio was 125:100:187, however, antler 
cast was assumed to be significant and the buck ratio 
is likely underestimated, while the fawn and doe ratio is 
underreported as deer tended to be in large groups 
during the survey that made individual classifications 
difficult. The estimated density was 1.171 white-tailed 
deer/km² (90% CI 0.800–1.716; CV = 23.3%) and 
estimated abundance was 2,564 white-tailed deer 
(90% CI 1,751–3,755; CV = 23.3%).
